replacement: Madame Hohlakov looked truly frightened. “This is serious, serious,” she kept repeating, every few words, as if nothing that had ever happened to her before had been serious. Alyosha listened unhappily and started to tell her what he had been through, but she cut him off after the first few words. She had no time to listen. She begged him to go and sit with Lise and wait there for her.

“Because if he’d taken the money, an hour after getting home he’d be weeping with mortification. That’s exactly what would have happened. And most likely he’d have come to me first thing tomorrow and maybe thrown the notes at me and trampled on them, as he did just now. But now he’s gone home terribly proud and triumphant, even though he knows he’s ‘ruined himself.’ So now nothing could be easier than getting him to accept the two hundred roubles by tomorrow, because he’s already proved his honor, tossed the money away and stamped on it.... He couldn’t know, when he did it, that I’d bring it to him again tomorrow, and yet he’s in terrible need of that money. Proud as he is of himself now, even today he’ll be thinking what a help he has lost. At night he’ll think about it more than ever and dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he may be ready to run to me and beg my forgiveness. And that’s just when I’ll turn up. ‘Look, you’re a proud man,’ I’ll say. ‘You’ve shown it; but now take the money and forgive us!’ And then he’ll take it!”
“Let’s, Lise; I’m ready. Though I’m not altogether ready in myself. Sometimes I’m very impatient, and other times I just don’t see things. It’s different with you.”

“Alyosha, we’ll have to put off kissing. We’re not ready for it yet, and we’ll be waiting a long time,” she finished suddenly. “Tell me instead: you’re so clever, so intellectual, so observant. Why do you pick a little idiot, an invalid like me? Oh, Alyosha, I’m awfully happy, because I don’t deserve you one bit.”

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he went on, “and my father too. And they’re destroying others along with them. It’s ‘the primitive force of the Karamazovs,’ as Father Païssy put it the other day: a crude, unbridled, earthly force. Does the spirit of God move over that force? Even that I don’t know. I only know that I, too, am a Karamazov.... Me a monk, a monk! Am I a monk, Lise? You said a moment ago that I was.”

“Now go. Christ be with you!” and she made the sign of the cross over him. “Hurry back to _him_ while he’s still alive. I see I’ve been cruel to keep you so long. I’ll pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we’ll be happy! Will we be happy? Will we?”
